Structural Properties of Shortest Flip Sequences Between Plane Spanning Trees

Oswin Aichholzer    Joseph Dorfer    Peter Kramer    Christian Rieck    Birgit Vogtenhuber
Abstract

We study the problem of reconfiguring non-crossing spanning trees on point sets in the plane in convex position. A flip is a reconfiguration step in which one edge of a tree is replaced with another, yielding again a non-crossing spanning tree. For a given point set PP, the flip graph has a vertex for each non-crossing spanning tree on PP, and an edge between any two trees that differ by a single flip. The flip distance between two trees is the length of a shortest path between them in the flip graph, that is, the minimum number of flips needed to transform one tree into the other.

We study structural properties of shortest flip sequences. Over the years, several conjectures have been proposed regarding these sequences. The folklore happy edge conjecture suggests that any edge shared by both the initial and target tree is never flipped in a shortest flip sequence. Moreover, the parking conjecture claims that in shortest flip sequences, every edge is either flipped to a target edge or parked on the convex hull. Notably, the happy edge conjecture is implied by the parking conjecture. Furthermore, it has been conjectured that an edge is never reparked, that is, any edge resulting from a flip either is a target edge or is subsequently flipped to a target edge. Essentially, all recent flip algorithms rely on these three conjectures and the properties they imply.

In this paper, we disprove both the parking and the reparking conjecture. In particular, we show that a flip sequence obeying the parking property sometimes needs linearly more flips than a shortest flip sequence, and exhibit examples where any shortest flip sequence flips some edge multiple times. In contrast, we identify several conditions under which the parking and reparking properties hold; these imply that the reparking property holds for compatible flips, and may be exploited by algorithms to obtain short flip sequences.

1 Introduction

Reconfiguration problems ask whether one feasible state of a system can be transformed into another through a sequence of allowed moves, a perspective made intuitive by classic puzzles such as the Rubik’s cube or the 15-puzzle. In the former, for instance, a single rotation of a face, either 90​° or 180​°, constitutes an elementary move, and sequences of such face rotations navigate a vast state space of about 4.3⋅10194.3\cdot 10^{19} reachable configurations. The structure of this state space, that is, how configurations are connected by allowed moves, is captured formally by the respective reconfiguration graph, where vertices represent configurations and edges correspond to single moves. Remarkably, despite its enormous size, the reconfiguration graph of the Rubik’s cube has diameter 2020, so any scrambled cube can be solved in at most 2020 face rotations. This viewpoint extends far beyond puzzles: in combinatorics, (computational) geometry, and theoretical computer science in general, reconfiguration graphs are a tool for studying families of objects that can be transformed into one another.

Another natural and illustrative example of geometric reconfiguration is the reconfiguration of triangulations of a convex point set. In this context, a flip is a local move that replaces one diagonal of a convex quadrilateral formed by two adjacent triangles with the other diagonal, thereby obtaining a new triangulation. The reconfiguration graph (also called flip graph) is the 11-skeleton of the associahedron. These triangulations are in bijection with binary trees [36], and each flip corresponds exactly to a rotation in the associated tree. Hence, the number of flips needed to transform one triangulation into another is the same as the number of rotations required to reorganize the corresponding binary trees. Since binary search trees are a fundamental data structure, understanding and minimizing these rotations is crucial for improving the efficiency of algorithms that rely on tree operations. Even though it is known that the diameter of the associahedron is equal to 2​n−62n-6 (for n≥11n\geq 11), it has remained an open problem whether there exists a polynomial-time algorithm for calculating the rotation distance [34, 36]. In a very recent preprint, Dorfer [20] answers this question in the negative.

In this paper, we consider the reconfiguration of non-crossing spanning trees on point sets in convex position. A flip in a non-crossing spanning tree removes one edge from the tree and adds another edge, resulting again in a non-crossing spanning tree. The corresponding flip graph has as vertices all non-crossing spanning trees on a convex set PP of nn points, and two vertices are connected by an edge precisely when the associated trees differ in a single flip. A flip sequence between two trees is any path in the flip graph from the vertex representing one tree to that representing the other tree, and the flip distance is the length of a shortest such path. See Figure 1 for the flip graph of plane spanning trees on 44 points in non-convex position.

Recent research has focused on (1) the diameter of the flip graph, that is, the maximum flip distance between any pair of trees on convex point sets and (2) algorithmic aspects of the computation of the flip distance. For over two decades, the benchmark results for bounds on the diameter were an upper and a lower bound of 2​n−42n-4 [11] and ⌊3​n2⌋−5\lfloor\frac{3n}{2}\rfloor-5 [24], respectively. The upper bound on the diameter was later improved to 2​n−log⁡(n)2n-\log(n) [1], and shortly after to 2​n−n2n-\sqrt{n} [18]. In [17], the longstanding 2​n2n barrier was surpassed by proving an upper bound on the diameter of ≈1.96​n\approx 1.96n. The currently best known bounds are a lower bound of (117−o⁡(1))​n(\frac{11}{7}-o(1))n by Bjerkevik, Dorfer, Kleist, Ueckerdt, and Vogtenhuber [13], and an upper bound of 5​n3−3\frac{5n}{3}-3 by Bjerkevik, Kleist, Ueckerdt, and Vogtenhuber [14].

One potentially useful tool for tackling the above two questions is the set of edges common to the start and target tree, known as happy edges. All other edges are referred to as unhappy. Building on this concept, the following long-standing conjecture is considered folklore.

Conjecture 1 (Happy edge conjecture).

Let TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} be two plane spanning trees, and let H=TI∩TFH=T_{I}\cap T_{F} be the set of all happy edges. Then there exists a shortest flip sequence TI=T0,T1,…,Tk−1,Tk=TFT_{I}=T_{0},T_{1},\ldots,T_{k-1},T_{k}=T_{F} such that H⊂TiH\subset T_{i} for every i∈[0,k]i\in[0,k].

Most of the aforementioned improvements to the diameter bounds are based on paths that respect this conjecture, that is, they never flip happy edges. Specifically, the authors of [1] present their 2​n−log⁡(n)2n-\log(n) bound as follows:

“…happy edges do not flip. An unhappy edge of TIT_{I} flips once or twice, and if twice, it flips to the convex hull and then to an edge of TFT_{F}.”

Moreover, they define as parking edges those edges that occur in some tree along a flip sequence but are absent from both the start and final tree and conjecture that parking on the convex hull is sufficient:

Conjecture 2 (Parking edge conjecture).

For any two plane spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F}, there exists a shortest flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} that uses only edges of TI∪TF∪𝖢𝖧T_{I}\cup T_{F}\cup{\mathsf{CH}}.

Although it was not explicitly stated as a conjecture, the above quote suggests that there always exists a shortest flip sequence in which every unhappy edge is flipped either once or twice, motivating the following conjecture.

Conjecture 3 (Reparking conjecture).

For any two plane spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F}, there exists a shortest flip sequence such that every parking edge is flipped to an edge of TFT_{F}. In particular, every edge is flipped at most twice.

This conjecture is further supported by the fact that, to date, every algorithm yielding a non-trivial upper bound on the diameter flips edges either directly to final edges, or first parks them on the convex hull, from where they are later flipped to final edges [1, 5, 14, 17, 18]; we refer to Table 1 for further details.

Some preliminary results and structural insights towards the three conjectures include the following: (i) The parking edge conjecture directly implies the happy edge conjecture [1], and (ii) the happy edge conjecture does not hold when the allowed flips are restricted to edge slides [1] or rotations [5]; see Section 2 for precise definitions. In contrast, (iii) the parking edge conjecture (and consequently the happy edge conjecture) holds for compatible flips [5]. For the case of unrestricted flips, the conjectures had remained open. The authors of [14], who established the best currently known upper bound on the diameter, describe their upper bound construction as follows:

“We note that the flip sequences we construct for [14, Theorem 26, arXiv-Version], which is our strongest upper bound, have both these properties [Conjecture 1 and Conjecture 2], providing some evidence in favor of the conjectures.”

1.1 Our contributions

We make progress towards the conjectures by uncovering structural insights in the different settings. This, in turn, sheds new light on the properties of shortest flip sequences between plane spanning trees on convex point sets. In particular, we obtain the following results.

First, we show a useful property of shortest flip sequences, namely that a flip is either final, or the removed edge would be crossed later in the sequence. Moreover, we show with Theorem 5 that the parking conjecture implies the reparking conjecture and that Conjecture 3 holds for compatible flips. Simultaneously, there always exists a shortest flip sequence in which every flip that removes a convex hull edge adds an edge of TFT_{F}.

Theorem 4 (Final flip property).

For any two plane spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F}, there exists a shortest flip sequence such that every flip is either final, or the removed edge is crossed by another edge later on.

Theorem 5.

Consider any two plane spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} of a point set PP.

  1. 1.

    There exists a shortest flip sequence such that any convex hull edge is flipped at most once.

  2. 2.

    In the compatible case, all edges are flipped at most twice (Compatible reparking property).

Further, we refute Conjecture 2 by demonstrating that, for certain instances, algorithms that only introduce parking edges on the convex hull produce sequences that are far from optimal. More precisely, we show:

Theorem 6.

There exists a family of trees (TI,k)k∈ℕ(T_{I,k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} and (TF,k)k∈ℕ(T_{F,k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} on 10​k+210k+2 vertices such that the length of the shortest flip sequence that only uses parking edges from the convex hull is at least by kk flips longer than the shortest possible flip sequence.

Finally, we disprove Conjecture 3 for the unrestricted case, obtaining the following:

Theorem 7.

There exist pairs of plane spanning trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F}, and TI′T^{\prime}_{I} and TF′T^{\prime}_{F} on 2222 and 3232 points, respectively, such that any shortest flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F}, respectively TI′T^{\prime}_{I} to TF′T^{\prime}_{F}, flips the same edge 33, respectively 44, times.

Outline.

We begin by summarizing additional related work in Section 1.2 and general definitions in Section 2. We then present our positive structural results in Section 3, before showing that, in general, neither the parking nor the reparking property holds for unrestricted flips in Sections 4.1 and 4.2, respectively.

Due to space constraints, proofs of statements marked with (⋆\star) are given in the appendix.

1.2 Further related work

Flip graphs of non-crossing configurations on planar point sets have been widely studied for other graph classes, including triangulations [8, 21, 22, 23, 27, 28, 31, 33, 34, 36], spanning paths [6, 7, 10, 29, 35], and matchings [2, 3, 12, 25, 26]; see also the survey by Bose and Hurtado [16]. Several of the aforementioned works rely on structural observations similar to the ones we present for plane spanning trees.

In [36], the authors establish the happy edge property for triangulations of convex point sets. Moreover, they demonstrate that a greedy strategy that adds edges of a target triangulation whenever possible, always produces a shortest flip sequence. These insights underpin several 𝖥𝖯𝖳\mathsf{FPT}-algorithms [15, 19, 30, 32], when the flip distance is a parameter. Conversely, the happy edge property does not hold for triangulations of point sets in general position [16], and counterexamples to it were key to the 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-hardness proofs in the case of point sets in general position [31, 33], as well as simple polygons [8].

Similarly, the flip distance problem for perfect matchings on point sets in general position has been proven to be 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-hard [12]. The proof likewise relies on counterexamples to the happy edge property. When the point set is restricted to be convex, the problem is polynomial-time solvable, as an edge from the target matching can always be inserted greedily [25].

Although the happy edge property does not hold, shortest flip sequences between plane paths on convex point sets can still be computed in polynomial time [6]; a key ingredient of the proof is the partitioning of happy edges into “good” and “bad” happy edges, which are then treated separately. Sometimes it is sufficient to consider only the happy edges on the convex hull; for example, convex hull edges satisfy the happy edge property in problems such as plane spanning trees [1], or odd matchings [2] on convex point sets. In both cases, this observation played a crucial role in deriving related 𝖥𝖯𝖳\mathsf{FPT}-algorithms [2, 5].

Beyond complexity results, counterexamples to the happy edge property have been generalized to establish a quadratic lower bound on the sliding distance between plane spanning trees on convex point sets [9].

2 Preliminaries

Throughout this paper, we denote by P⊂ℝ2P\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} a set of nn points in convex position, that is, a set PP such that no point p∈Pp\in P is a convex combination of any three other points. For a pair of points u,v∈Pu,v\in P, we denote by u​vuv the straight-line segment connecting the two. If uu and vv are adjacent on the convex hull of PP, we call u​vuv a convex hull edge and write u​v∈𝖢𝖧uv\in{\mathsf{CH}}. A plane spanning tree of PP is then a set of n−1n-1 edges T⊂(P2)T\subset\binom{P}{2} that forms a tree such that the edges’ line segments are pairwise disjoint or meet at a common endpoint. We denote the removal and insertion of an edge ee by T−eT-e and T+eT+e, using standard set notation otherwise.

Flip.

A flip in TT removes an edge e∈Te\in T and adds an edge f∉Tf\notin T such that the resulting structure T−e+fT-e+f is again a plane spanning tree. If the initial tree TT is clear from context, we denote this operation by e→fe\rightarrow f and write that ee is flipped to ff. We differentiate between four types of flips; a flip e→fe\rightarrow f is compatible if the straight-line segments ee and ff are either disjoint or share a common endpoint, and crossing otherwise. For u,v,w∈Pu,v,w\in P, a compatible flip of the shape u​v→u​wuv\rightarrow uw is called a rotation, and furthermore called a slide if v​w∈Tvw\in T. Examples of all types of flips can be seen in Figure 2.

Flip graph.

The flip graph of plane spanning trees of PP is the graph that has all such trees as its vertices. Two spanning trees share an edge in the flip graph if and only if they can be transformed into one another via a single flip. Given a pair of trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F}, a flip sequence 𝒮\mathcal{S} from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} is then a path in the flip graph denoted by a sequence of trees TI=T0,T1,…,Tk−1,Tk=TF{T_{I}=T_{0},T_{1},\ldots,T_{k-1},T_{k}=T_{F}} such that consecutive trees only differ by a single flip; its length is the number kk of flips in the sequence. The flip distance of TIT_{I} and TFT_{F}, denoted by d⁡(TI,TF)d(T_{I},T_{F}), is the length of a shortest sequence. Furthermore, the edges TI∩TFT_{I}\cap T_{F} are happy, with all other edges being unhappy. If a flip introduces an edge f∉TFf\notin T_{F}, it is commonly referred to as a parking flip, and ff as its parking edge. The diameter of a flip graph denotes the maximum flip distance between any pair of trees.

Trace.

We introduce additional notation to analyze flip sequences. Namely, we introduce structures that allow us to not only represent changes within trees under flip operations, but also how these flip operations affect individual edges. Given a flip sequence 𝒮=T0,…,Tk\mathcal{S}=T_{0},\ldots,T_{k}, we define the trace of an edge e∈T0e\in T_{0} as the ordered sequence of positions that it is flipped to; an example is shown in Figure 2. Formally, this corresponds to a tuple of edges:

trace⁡(e,𝒮)=trace⁡(e,T0,…,Tk)={(e)if k=0,trace⁡(e,T1,…,Tk)if e∈T0∩T1, or(e)∥trace⁡(f,T1,…,Tk)if {e,f}=T0​Δ​T1.\operatorname{trace}(e,\mathcal{S})=\operatorname{trace}(e,T_{0},\ldots,T_{k})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{@{}l@{}l@{\quad}l}(e)&&\text{if $k=0$,}\\ &\operatorname{trace}(e,T_{1},\ldots,T_{k})&\text{if $e\in T_{0}\cap T_{1}$, or}\\ (e)\parallel&\operatorname{trace}(f,T_{1},\ldots,T_{k})&\text{if $\{e,f\}=T_{0}\Delta T_{1}$.}\end{array}\right.

We say that the length of a trace is the number of flips in it, which corresponds to the number of elements minus one: The trace (e1,…,eℓ)(e_{1},\ldots,e_{\ell}) corresponds to the flips ei→ei+1e_{i}\to e_{i+1} for 1≤i<ℓ1\leq i<\ell. Observe that the length of 𝒮\mathcal{S} is exactly the sum of all trace lengths. A flip e→fe\to f in 𝒮\mathcal{S} is final if the trace of ff on the remaining sequence is (f)(f), and non-final otherwise. A happy edge e∈T0∩Tke\in T_{0}\cap T_{k} is fixed in the flip sequence 𝒮\mathcal{S} if it has trace length zero, or equivalently trace⁡(e,𝒮)=(e)\operatorname{trace}(e,\mathcal{S})=(e). This induces two properties of happy edges based on shortest flip sequences. A happy edge is weakly fixed if it is fixed in some shortest flip sequence, and strongly fixed if this applies to all such sequences.

We note that Conjectures 1, 2 and 3 can also be stated in terms of trace properties: The happy edge conjecture (Conjecture 1) states that all happy edges are weakly fixed. Similarly, the parking conjecture (Conjecture 2) states that there always exists a shortest flip sequence in which all but the first and final element of all traces are in 𝖢𝖧\mathsf{CH}, and the re-parking conjecture (Conjecture 3) states the existence of a shortest flip sequence in which each edge of TIT_{I} has trace length at most two.

3 Positive results on structural properties

We generalize a property shown by Aichholzer, Dorfer, and Vogtenhuber [5, Lemma 20]. They showed that in every compatible flip sequence any parking flip that parks on a diagonal can be replaced with a parking flip that parks on the convex hull. Actually, it is not required that the entire flip sequence is compatible, but only either the flip that inserts the parking edge or the flip that removes the parking edge has to be compatible. This already follows from their proof. For the sake of self-containment, we include the adapted proof and rewrite the statement in terms of our definitions.

Lemma 8 (⋆\star).

Let there be a flip sequence between two trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} and an edge ee such that t​r​a​c​e​(e)=(e,f,e′)trace(e)=(e,f,e^{\prime}), where ff is a diagonal and either the flip e→fe\to f or the flip f→e′{f\to e^{\prime}} is compatible. Then there exists a flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} of the same length in which t​r​a​c​e​(e)=(e,h,e′)trace(e)=(e,h,e^{\prime}) such that hh is a convex hull edge. The trace of any other edge remains unchanged.

In order to study the reparking property, we start by observing sufficient properties for edges to have trace length 11 or, equivalently, necessary conditions for an edge to have larger trace length.

Let TI=T0T_{I}=T_{0}, T1,…,Tk=TFT_{1},\ldots,T_{k}=T_{F} be such a flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F}. This concept has since been modified for matchings [25] and trees [1, Proposition 18], which we further adapt. For trees, a normalization is applied to a flip sequence and defined with respect to an edge ee that is not crossed by any other edge that is part of this flip sequence. For Property (3), observe that as long as in step kk there is an edge fk≠ef_{k}\neq e in the cycle ckc_{k} that is later on flipped, ee is part of the tree N⁡(Tk)N(T_{k}). Consider the last flip in 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N} for which an edge is added to ckc_{k} for some kk. Then in this flip ee was removed from N⁡(Tk)N(T_{k}) and flipped to an edge in the cycle ckc_{k}. As now the cycle ckc_{k} consists entirely of edges which are not flipped anymore in the remainder of 𝒮\mathcal{S}, Property (3) follows.

With the new flip sequence N⁡(T0)N(T_{0}), N⁡(T1),…,N⁡(Tk−1)N(T_{1}),\ldots,N(T_{k-1}), N⁡(Tk)N(T_{k}) we have made sure that ee is no longer an edge that is flipped multiple times, but not crossed at any point of the flip sequence. However, we might have introduced another edge with these properties in the new flip sequence. If no such edge exists then we are done. Thus for the remainder of the proof we assume that yet another edge is flipped multiple times but not crossed by any other edge of the flip sequence N⁡(T0)N(T_{0}), N⁡(T1),…,N⁡(Tk−1)N(T_{1}),\ldots,N(T_{k-1}), N⁡(Tk)N(T_{k}). In order to be able to show that Theorem 4 holds for all edges at the same time we, resort to a technique used in [5, Lemma 20].

If an edge s=a​bs=ab is contained in all trees of a flip sequence, then ss splits the convex point set into two sides AA and BB, the vertices that appear in clockwise order between aa and bb and the vertices that appear in counterclockwise order. The vertices aa and bb count towards both, side AA and side BB. For every tree, we obtain two subtrees, the induced subtrees on AA and BB. Every flip in one of the trees is completely independent of the flips in the other side. Thus, we can interleave both ordered subsequences that flip edges in only one of the two sides to obtain a valid flip sequence with the same initial and final trees. We will use this to argue that the only flip in trace⁡(e,𝒮N)\operatorname{trace}(e,\mathcal{S}_{N}), denoted by e→ge\to g, is independent of all subsequent flips in 𝒮N\mathcal{S}_{N}. This will then imply that e→ge\to g can be performed as the last flip.

To this end, assume that the flip from N⁡(Ti)N(T_{i}) to N⁡(Ti+1)N(T_{i+1}) is the final flip that removes ee and inserts gg. We split the convex point set along all edges of ci+1∖{e,g}c_{i+1}\setminus\{e,g\}. Every tree N⁡(Ti),N⁡(Ti+1),…,N⁡(Tk)N(T_{i}),N(T_{i+1}),\ldots,N(T_{k}) now splits into |ci+1|−1\lvert c_{i+1}\rvert-1 trees by splitting along the edges of ci+1∖{e,g}c_{i+1}\setminus\{e,g\} (recall that cj=ci+1c_{j}=c_{i+1} for any j≥i+1j\geq i+1). Flip sequences of these trees in the resulting subsets are independent of another and can be interleaved in any order.

After splitting the point set, there exists a particular subset CC, as depicted in Figure 4, of vertices that contains the vertices of both, ee and gg. By the previous discussion, we can perform the flip sequence in CC, that also performs the flip e→ge\to g, as the last flip sequence among all flip sequences in the subsets.

It remains to argue that we can perform the flip e→ge\to g as the last flip in CC. For this, we argue that all other flips can be performed, independently of whether ee or gg is present in the current tree. CC has three parts for which ee and gg form the border: The side CeC_{e} of ee that does not contain gg, the side CgC_{g} of gg that does not contain ee, and the part between ee and gg. The latter part contains exactly the edges of ci+1c_{i+1}. Therefore, no flips other than e→ge\to g happen in this part, since no edge of ci+1c_{i+1} is flipped.

Consider a flip in CeC_{e}. If we want to flip h′→g′h^{\prime}\to g^{\prime} in CeC_{e} then, when adding g′g^{\prime} to the involved tree in CeC_{e}, we obtain a cycle ch′,g′c_{h^{\prime},g^{\prime}} that contains h′h^{\prime} and g′g^{\prime}. If ch′,g′c_{h^{\prime},g^{\prime}} contains neither ee nor gg, then obviously it does not matter if we perform the flip h′→g′h^{\prime}\to g^{\prime} before of after e→ge\to g. If one of ee or gg is in ch′,g′c_{h^{\prime},g^{\prime}} (note that it is not possible that both are in the cycle at the same time), then we argue that they can be replaced by each other. The alternative cycle containing g′g^{\prime} and h′h^{\prime} is then the symmetric difference of ch′,g′c_{h^{\prime},g^{\prime}} and ci+1c_{i+1}, namely c^h′,g′=ch′,g′​Δ​ci+1\hat{c}_{h^{\prime},g^{\prime}}=c_{h^{\prime},g^{\prime}}\Delta c_{i+1}. See Figure 4 for an example. If ch′,g′c_{h^{\prime},g^{\prime}} contains the edge ee, then c^h′,g′\hat{c}_{h^{\prime},g^{\prime}} contains the detour via ci+1∖{e}c_{i+1}\setminus\{e\}, including gg. Vice, versa if ch′,g′c_{h^{\prime},g^{\prime}} contains gg, and thus ci+1∖{e}c_{i+1}\setminus\{e\}, then c^h′,g′\hat{c}_{h^{\prime},g^{\prime}} contains ee. For flips in CgC_{g} we argue symmetrically.

To finally prove the theorem, we conclude that we can reorder the flips in the flip sequence such that the flip e→ge\to g, which is a final flip, is the last flip of the flip sequence. As ee was an edge of the initial tree TIT_{I} and has now trace length 1, we can remove the flip e→ge\to g from our sequence without changing whether the conditions of Theorem 4 are fulfilled. Therefore, by omitting the flip e→ge\to g and adjusting the target tree accordingly to Tk+e−gT_{k}+e-g, we have produced a flip sequence that is one flip shorter than our initial sequence. Recall that we assumed that an edge that is flipped multiple times but not crossed by any other edge was introduced to the sequence N⁡(T0)N(T_{0}), N⁡(T1),…,N⁡(Tk−1)N(T_{1}),\ldots,N(T_{k-1}), N⁡(Tk)N(T_{k}). Thus our new, shorter, flip sequence also contains that edge. This provides a contradiction to our assumption that the flip sequence from the start was the one with the minimum number of flips among all sequences that do not fulfill the statement of the theorem. ∎

We continue by showing that Theorem 4 is strong enough to settle the reparking property for compatible flip sequences, as well as for convex hull edges of TIT_{I} in the general case.

See 5

Proof.

The first part follows from the fact that convex hull edges are never crossed together with Theorem 4.

For the second part we apply that the parking property holds for compatible flips [5, Lemma 20]. Since there exists a shortest flip sequence that only introduces parking edges on the convex hull, we can apply part (1) of this theorem to the parking edges on the convex hull. Every edge is then flipped at most twice: once to park on the convex hull and once for the final flip. ∎

Corollary 9.

For every pair of trees TIT_{I}, TFT_{F}, there exists a shortest flip sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} in which every flip that removes a diagonal ee adds one of the three following:

  • •

    An edge of TFT_{F} via a final flip.

  • •

    An edge on the convex hull.

  • •

    A parking edge that crosses ee.

Further, any flip that removes a convex hull edge is final.

Proof.

The only case left is when a diagonal ee is replaced by a non-crossing diagonal. By Lemma 8, there exists an alternative flip sequence that replaces ee with a convex hull edge. ∎

4 Counterexamples for general flips

In the previous section, we identified structural conditions that any counterexample to the parking and reparking conjectures must satisfy for general flips. With these conditions in hand, we now construct specific pairs of trees, TIT_{I} and TFT_{F}, that not only meet these requirements but also go further, yielding shortest flip sequences that violate the conjectures.

Through a combination of case distinctions, additional observations on flip sequences, and support from a computer program, we verify that the proposed flip sequences are indeed the shortest possible flip sequences. Moreover, we demonstrate that no alternative shortest flip sequence can satisfy the conjectures.

4.1 The parking edge property

In this section, we prove Theorem 6, thereby disproving Conjecture 2. The theorem consists of two parts, which we state and prove separately for convenience.

Lemma 10 (⋆\star).

The parking edge conjecture does not hold for general flips and n≥12n\geq 12 points in convex position. Moreover, a minimum counterexample need not be restricted to incompatible flips, and may even contain edge slides in all shortest flip sequences.

Proof sketch.

Consider the pair of trees visualized in Figure 5. Our aim is to transform TIT_{I} into TFT_{F}. In doing so, we demonstrate that all shortest flip sequences must necessarily park an edge on a diagonal. In Figure 6, we depict a flip sequence that uses a diagonal parking edge p1p_{1} (green). Moreover, it requires exactly one parking flip, e1→p1e_{1}\to p_{1}, while all other flips are final. Furthermore, since every edge in the symmetric difference TI​Δ​TFT_{I}\Delta T_{F} is crossed at least twice, the first flip of any sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} must necessarily be a parking flip. Therefore, the sequence illustrated in Figure 6 is indeed a shortest flip sequence. We note that this flip sequence does also contain two edge slides; these are highlighted in purple.

It remains to show that any parking flip that parks to the convex hull instead of p1p_{1} requires at least one additional flip. To this end, we show that no flip sequence beginning with a parking flip to the convex hull can reach TFT_{F} exclusively using final flips thereafter. In Figures 6 to 6, we indicate all possible first flips (up to symmetry) that replace a diagonal of TI∖TFT_{I}\setminus T_{F} with an edge on the convex hull. For each such flip, Figure 6 depicts a flip sequence that continues performing perfect flips until it becomes impossible to add any further edge of the final tree without making another parking flip. We emphasize that these sequences are not unique, as sometimes multiple edges can be flipped to the same edge, or flips can be performed in a different order yet still produce the same result. For instance, Figure 7 shows the graph of all possible sequences that start with e2→g8{e_{2}\to g_{8}} and otherwise consist of final flips. The same reasoning applies to the other cases in which a diagonal is parked on the convex hull, as each can be analyzed in a similar manner.

∎

To compute all relevant flip sequences for the example shown in Figure 5, we employ a straightforward computer program [4], which systematically generates and tracks all possible sequences. The program initializes a set of edges with the edges of the initial tree TIT_{I} and then simply works in a depth first search (DFS) like manner. For every given set of edges it considers all possible legal flips (such that after the flip the set of edges still forms a spanning tree). For each such flip, it performs the flip and then increases a counter in case that this flip was not perfect, that is, did not insert an edge of the final tree. Only if this counter does not exceed the maximum allowed number of non-perfect flips (one in our case) the program continues recursively. Otherwise the flip is undone and the next legal flip is performed, etc. Whenever all edges of the set are from the final tree TFT_{F} another counter for the number of shortest flip sequences is increased. The program terminates once the DFS is completed.

For the trees shown in Figure 5 the output of the program gives 2020 different flip sequences of length 8. That these are indeed precisely all the sequences which contain the parking flip e1→p1{e_{1}\to p_{1}} can be verified by counting all shortest flip sequences depicted in Figure 12. Observe that there is some left-right symmetry once the flip e1→p1{e_{1}\to p_{1}} has been made. Then the flips e2→f4{e_{2}\to f_{4}}, e3→f3{e_{3}\to f_{3}}, and e4→f2{e_{4}\to f_{2}} have to be performed in that order, but can interleave with the symmetric flips e2¯→f4¯{\overline{e_{2}}\to\overline{f_{4}}}, e3¯→f3¯{\overline{e_{3}}\to\overline{f_{3}}}, and e4¯→f2¯{\overline{e_{4}}\to\overline{f_{2}}} in an arbitrary order. As this is the only place where the order is flexible, we get (63)=20{6\choose 3}=20 different flip sequences of length 8, precisely the number reported by the program.

We used a modified version of our program to generate the relevant flip graph, that is, all trees and flips between them that can be reached from the initial tree TIT_{I} with a flip sequence that includes at most one non-perfect flip. This graph has 118 different trees as nodes, and 214 edges (flips) between them. The full graph is depicted in Figure 12 in Appendix C.

We further reduced these numbers by forcing the first (non-perfect) flip to be a flip onto the convex hull. This is possible because to verify the correctness of our statement, we only need to consider shortest flip sequences that do not have a parking flip to a diagonal (recall that the first flip has to be a parking flip). This results in a graph with only 67 trees and 120 edges which nicely shows all relevant cases, including the one elaborated in detail in the proof of Lemma 10. Both variants of the flip graph can be interactively explored [4].

For the reader’s convenience, all relevant components of the graph can be found in Appendix C alongside Figure 12; each possible parking flip leads to a unique (up to symmetry) portion of the subgraph that remains reachable without making a second non-perfect flip. These can be found in Figures 7, 15, 13 and 14.

Restricting flips to parking edges on the convex hull incurs a single additional flip, as we have seen in Figure 5. We next strengthen this result, proving the existence of instances that require Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) additional flips under the same constraint.

Lemma 11.

For any k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, there exist two non-crossing spanning trees on n≥10​k+2n\geq 10k+2 points such that a shortest flip sequence takes 8​k8k flips, whereas a shortest flip sequence that parks only on convex hull edges takes at least 9​k9k flips.

Proof.

We glue kk instances of trees TIT_{I} as seen in Figure 5 along happy edges. Our target structure consists of kk instances of TFT_{F} glued along the same happy edges. If no happy edges are flipped in a flip sequence this is equivalent to having kk separate flip sequences in every individual occurrence of TIT_{I} and we need 88 flips in an optimal flip sequence compared to 99 if we only use parking edges on the convex hull. Summing over all occurrences of TIT_{I} gives an optimal flip sequence of length 8​k8k and a minimum flip distance when only using parking edges on the convex hull of 9​k9k.

Next, assume for a minimum counterexample that all k−1k-1 consecutive happy edges are removed at some point during the flip sequence and added back in a later flip. We argue that this flip sequence has to take at least 10​k−210k-2 flips, unless it introduces parking edges that are not on the convex hull. Assume the opposite. Now, the flip sequence removes and adds happy edges and since the flip sequence does not introduce diagonal parking edges, the happy edges are never crossed by any edge during the flip sequence. Proposition 18 in [1] states that in any minimum flip sequence, for any happy edge that is removed there later has to exist some edge that would have crossed this happy edge. If such a crossing edge does not exist, the proof of the proposition gives a construction of a flip sequence that is at least one flip shorter and that does not remove the happy edge. By applying this result, we can iteratively construct flip sequences that do not remove and add one happy edge such that the resulting flip sequence is by one flip shorter than the original flip sequence. Applying the result iteratively for all happy edges, gives a flip sequence of length at most 9​k−19k-1 that does not flip any happy edges and still does not use any parking edges outside the convex hull. By the pigeonhole principle, there exists one occurrence of TIT_{I} that is flipped to an occurrence of TFT_{F} in only 88 flips without introducing diagonal parking edges, contradicting Lemma 10. ∎

On the positive side, we demonstrate that flip sequences that park solely on the convex hull remain close to an optimal flip sequence. More precisely, we prove that a diagonal parking flip can be replaced by two convex hull parking flips. Applying the following proposition once for every diagonal parking flip yields a flip sequence without any parking flip, but at the cost of one additional flip per iteration.

Proposition 12.

A flip sequence that adds and removes a parking diagonal dd by non-compatible flips can be replaced with a flip sequence that does not perform a diagonal parking flip that involves dd and that is only one flip longer. In particular, the resulting flip sequence performs strictly fewer diagonal parking flips than the original one.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, assume that in the flip from TI=T0T_{I}=T_{0} to T1T_{1} an edge ee is flipped to a parking edge f=(va,vb)f=(v_{a},v_{b}) via a non-compatible flip and in the flip from Tk−1T_{k-1} to Tk=TFT_{k}=T_{F} ff is removed by a non-compatible flip and exchanged for an edge e′e^{\prime}. Then, ff separates the point set into two sides AA and BB, the points that appear in clockwise order from vav_{a} to vbv_{b}, and the points in counterclockwise order. We include vav_{a} and vbv_{b} in both sets. In the flip sequence from T1T_{1} to Tk−1T_{k-1} flips that exchange edges in AA or BB can be executed independently from the other side. If we remove the edge ff from T1T_{1}, we obtain two subtrees and there exists a convex hull edge between two consecutive convex hull vertices vi,vi+1v_{i},v_{i+1} in AA that connects the two subtrees. Without loss of generality viv_{i} lies in the same subtree as vav_{a}.

We flip from T0T_{0} to (T1∖{f})∪{h}(T_{1}\setminus\{f\})\cup\{h\}. Then any flip in the flip sequence from T1T_{1} to Tk−1T_{k-1} that happens in side BB can still be executed. Any flip that added and removed an edge that bounded a cycle that contains ff now contains a path that walks first from vav_{a} to viv_{i} to the subtree in AA, then traverses hh and later moves from vi+1v_{i+1} to vbv_{b}.

After all flips in BB have been executed and the side BB coincides with the side BB in Tk−1T_{k-1}, we perform a flip that removes hh and adds a convex hull edge h′h^{\prime} that joins the two resulting subtrees in BB. We continue to execute all flips in side AA. Again, any flip that involves a cycle that contains ff now contains a path through side BB and the convex hull edge h′h^{\prime}. After performing all flips in AA, we reached the tree Tk−1∖{f}∪{h}{T_{k-1}\setminus\{f\}\cup\{h\}}. As a last flip, we remove hh and add e′e^{\prime} to obtain the tree TkT_{k}. We made all the flips that happened in the original flip sequence. Only the trace of edge ee has been changed from (e,f,e′)(e,f,e^{\prime}) to (e,h,h′,e′)(e,h,h^{\prime},e^{\prime}). Therefore, the resulting flip sequence is exactly one flip longer than the original flip sequence. ∎

We note that the flip sequence derived due to the proof of Proposition 12 is not “nice”, in the sense that it includes a non-final flip from one convex hull edge to another. Using Theorem 4, we can reorder certain flips, producing a “nicer” flip sequence.

4.2 The reparking property

From Theorems 4 and 8, we derive necessary conditions for a counterexample to the reparking property as follows:

Proposition 13.

Suppose there exists a shortest flip sequence with an edge ee with t​r​a​c​e​(e)=(e,e1,e2,e3)trace(e)=(e,e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}) of length 33. If no other shortest flip sequence exists in which ee has shorter trace, the following conditions must hold:

(1)

ee and e3e_{3} are diagonals.

(2)

ee and e1e_{1} cross.

(3)

e1e_{1} and e2e_{2} cross.

(4)

e2e_{2} and e3e_{3} cross.

Proof.

We approach the different conditions one by one.

(1)

If ee is a convex hull edge, it is in particular not intersected by any other edge. By Theorem 4, we conclude that there exists a shortest flip sequence that flips ee to its final position. If e3e_{3} is a convex hull edge, we apply Theorem 4 to the reversed flip sequence.

(2)

If ee and e1e_{1} do not cross, then e1e_{1} is added by a compatible flip. We can apply Lemma 8 to obtain a shortest flip sequence in which e1e_{1} is replaced by a convex hull edge. In a second step, we apply Theorem 4 to obtain a shortest flip sequence in which e1e_{1} is flipped to its final position. Therefore, we have constructed a shortest flip sequence in which ee has trace length 22.

(3)

If e1e_{1} and e2e_{2} do not cross, we first apply Lemma 8 to obtain a shortest flip sequence in which e2e_{2} is replaced with a convex hull edge h2h_{2}. Now we can reverse the flip sequence. In the new flip sequence e3e_{3} is flipped to a convex hull edge. Then, we apply Theorem 4 to obtain a shortest flip sequence in which h2h_{2} is flipped to its final position in the reversed flip sequence, that is, ee. By reversing the flip sequence again, we obtain a shortest flip sequence in which t​r​a​c​e​(e)=(e,h2,e3)trace(e)=(e,h_{2},e_{3}), in particular, ee has trace length 22.

(4)

If e2e_{2} and e3e_{3} do not cross, we reverse the flip sequence and proceed as in Case (2).∎

Figure 9 provides a counterexample towards the reparking property. This counterexample was constructed with the conditions of Proposition 13 in mind. Any shortest flip sequence from TIT_{I} in red to TFT_{F} in blue contains an edge with trace length 33. A sketch of a shortest flip sequence is given in Figure 10. First, the central diagonal in red is flipped to the green diagonal. Then, we can perform six perfect flips that insert edges from TFT_{F}. Afterwards, the green diagonal is flipped again. We can perform six additional perfect flips, before we can flip the green edge to its final position.

The flip sequence sketched in Figure 10 is the unique shortest flip sequence (up to ordering) of the six perfect flips that occur between consecutive flips that involve the green edge. To verify this, we again used our program [4]. Here the relevant part of the flip graph has 5086 vertices (which are at most two non-perfect flips away from TIT_{I}). The size of this graph seems thus to be rather challenging for human inspection. As we saw already for the proof of Lemma 10 that a hand written case distinction will be too tedious we rely here on the program. It generated a total of 400400 shortest flip sequences which is precisely (63)⋅(63)\binom{6}{3}\cdot\binom{6}{3}, that is, the number of different orders how the perfect flips between parking flips can interleave.

We even took the construction one step further and provide a pair of trees in which for every shortest flip sequence there exists an edge that has trace length four, that is, it is two times reparked. The example is depicted in Figure 11. The edges in red are part of TIT_{I}, edges in blue are part of TFT_{F}, and the black edges on the convex hull are contained in both trees. We verified our example with the same program used for the two previous counterexamples.

5 Conclusions and future work

We established counterexamples to the parking and reparking properties for shortest flip sequences in the general setting, while proving that the reparking property holds when flips are restricted to be compatible. These results clarify the limits of existing assumptions and point to several promising directions for future research.

  • •

    In Table 1 we summarized all recent upper bounds on the diameter and specify which of the investigated properties each bound respects. Most notably, in every case the trace length of all edges is bounded from above by 22. This raises two questions: Will our constructions need to be incorporated to achieve further improvements in the upper bounds on the diameter of the flip graph, and do these counterexamples offer new insights for constructing tighter lower bounds?

  • •

    By disproving the parking conjecture for general flips, we have eliminated a previously promising approach of establishing the happy edge conjecture. Consequently, we think that entirely new methods are required to make further progress on that conjecture.

  • •

    We provided a construction of initial and final trees where every shortest flip sequence for these pairs has an edge of trace length 33 or 44, respectively. We expect that this construction can be iterated without limit. Thus, we raise the following conjecture:

Conjecture 14.

For any constant cc there exists a pair of trees TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} such that any shortest flip sequence between TIT_{I} and TFT_{F} has an edge with trace length larger than cc.

  • •

    Very recently it was shown that computing shortest (compatible) flip sequences between plane spanning trees of convex point sets is 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-complete [13] by Bjerkevik, Dorfer, Kleist, Ueckerdt, and Vogtenhuber. This highlights the importance of identifying effective 𝖥𝖯𝖳\mathsf{FPT}- or approximation algorithms. Can the reparking property for compatible flips be exploited to enhance the currently known 𝖥𝖯𝖳\mathsf{FPT}-algorithm of [5]? Moreover, our counterexamples to the parking and reparking properties may be instrumental in establishing higher intractability results.

Appendix A Omitted details from Section 3

See 8

Proof.

Without loss of generality, let e→fe\to f be the first and f→e′f\to e^{\prime} the last flip of the flip sequence. Further let e→fe\to f be a compatible flip, otherwise look at the reversed flip sequence. We denote with vav_{a} and vbv_{b} the two vertices of ff.

We reorder and modify the other flips based on the following observation. The edge ff separates the point set into two sides AA and BB, the points that appear in clockwise direction from vav_{a} to vbv_{b} and the points that appear in counterclockwise order, including vav_{a} and vbv_{b} in both AA and BB. While ff is part of the tree, flips in the two sides can be executed independently from the other side. Note that every spanning tree contains a unique path between any two vertices. If, in particular, we consider the path pp from vav_{a} to vbv_{b} in TI=T0T_{I}=T_{0}, we see that this path has to be contained entirely in one side induced by ff, w.l.o.g. in side BB. Otherwise, there would be an edge along the path that crosses ff, introducing a non-compatible flip from TIT_{I} to T1T_{1}.

If we add the edge ff, the cycle that gets closed is entirely contained in BB. Therefore, ee lies in BB. Any flip that is executed from T1T_{1} to Tk−1T_{k-1} that happens in AA can already be executed in TIT_{I}. Any cycle that previously involved the edge ff now involves the path pp instead. We order our flips in a way, such that all flips that happen in AA are executed right away starting from TIT_{I}. After executing all those steps, the side AA already coincides with the side AA in TFT_{F}, except for the edge ff.

Let us take a closer look at the part of TFT_{F} that lies in AA. This part consists of ff and two trees TT and T′T^{\prime} (possibly with an empty set of edges) in AA. Since TFT_{F} is plane there exist a unique pair of points that appear consecutively along the boundary of the convex hull and one belongs to TT and the other to T′T^{\prime}. We continue our modified flip sequence by adding the convex hull edge hh between those two points and removing the edge that would have been removed when adding ff.

Now we execute all the flips in BB from the original flip sequence. Any flip that formed a cycle that involves ff now forms a cycle that involves hh and paths in AA connecting vav_{a} and vbv_{b} to hh.

As a last flip we perform h→e′h\to e^{\prime} and reach the final tree TFT_{F}. The trace of ee is (e,h,e′)(e,h,e^{\prime}) and for any other edge in TIT_{I} the trace did not change between the two flip sequences. ∎

Appendix B Omitted details from Section 4

See 10

Proof.

Consider the pair of trees TIT_{I}, TFT_{F} depicted in Figure 5. In Figure 6, a sequence using a diagonal parking edge p1p_{1} (green) needs exactly one parking flip, e1→p1e_{1}\to p_{1}, while all other flips are final. Further, note that the first flip of any sequence from TIT_{I} to TFT_{F} must be a parking flip since every edge in the symmetric difference TI​Δ​TFT_{I}\Delta T_{F} is crossed at least twice. Hence the sequence depicted in Figure 6 is a shortest flip sequence. We note that this flip sequence does also contain two edge slides. These are highlighted in purple.

To prove the statement, it remains to show that any parking flip that parks to the convex hull instead of p1p_{1} requires at least one more flip. To do so, we show that no flip sequence that starts with a parking flip to the convex hull can reach TFT_{F} by performing only final flips after this parking flip. In Figures 6 to 6, we hint at all the possible first flips that remove one diagonal of TI∖TFT_{I}\setminus T_{F} add an edge on the convex hull instead. In every case we depict one flip sequence that performs perfect flips for as long as possible until no other edge of TFT_{F} can be added without performing another parking flip. We will refer to such flip sequences as maximal flip sequences.

The flip sequences in Figure 6 do not cover all cases that could possibly occur, since there are sometimes multiple edges that can be flipped to the same edge or multiple flips that can be executed in a different order while leading to the same result. For the case where the first flip is e2→g8{e_{2}\to g_{8}} a graph depicting all possible maximal flip sequences can be seen in Figure 7. All the other cases in which a diagonal is parked on the convex hull can be argued similarly. Since already the first case highlights how tedious the resulting case distinction is, we will resort to two different approaches to cover all cases. All the arguments in the case distinction boil down to three basic arguments: (1) If an edge of TFT_{F} is crossed at least twice, then it cannot be added by a single flip. (2) If an edge of TFT_{F} is crossed exactly once, then the only flip that could potentially add that edge is the flip that removes the edge that crosses it. (3) We cannot add edges of TFT_{F} if adding the edge would create a cycle in the graph. In all cases, the cycle will contain a parking edge on the convex hull.

After the proof, we will discuss how we checked all cases via a simple program [4] and provide a directed acyclic graph [4] that embeds all flip sequences that can be made with 88 flips where at most one of the flips can be a parking flip.

Back to the flip sequences starting with e2→g8{e_{2}\to g_{8}}. On the top, the initial tree is depicted, followed by the tree resulting from the flip e2→g8{e_{2}\to g_{8}}. There are only two edges of TFT_{F} that are not crossed twice, namely f4f_{4} and f3f_{3}, which are both crossed by the edge e2e_{2}. Flipping e1→f3{e_{1}\to f_{3}} will disconnect the tree so the only valid flip is e1→f4{e_{1}\to f_{4}}.

For the next flip, we have multiple edges of TFT_{F} that can be inserted, since f3f_{3} is not crossed at all and the edges f4¯\overline{f_{4}}, and f3¯\overline{f_{3}} are only crossed by e2¯\overline{e_{2}}. To insert f3f_{3} the three flips e3→f3{e_{3}\to f_{3}}, e2¯→f3{\overline{e_{2}}\to f_{3}}, and g8→f3{g_{8}\to f_{3}} are possible. To insert f3¯\overline{f_{3}}, we can perform the flip e2¯→f3{\overline{e_{2}}\to f_{3}}. Note that no flip can add the edge f4¯\overline{f_{4}} since f4¯\overline{f_{4}} is crossed by e2¯\overline{e_{2}} and flipping e2¯→f4¯{\overline{e_{2}}\to\overline{f_{4}}} creates a cycle.

In the left tree of the fourth row, there are three edges in TFT_{F} that are crossed by a single edge of TIT_{I}. More precisely, f2f_{2} is only crossed by e4e_{4} and f3¯\overline{f_{3}} is only crossed by e2¯\overline{e_{2}}. Similarly, also f4¯\overline{f_{4}} is only crossed by e2¯\overline{e_{2}}, but directly flipping e2¯→f4¯{\overline{e_{2}}\to\overline{f_{4}}} creates a cycle. We can perform the flips e4→f2{e_{4}\to f_{2}} and e2¯→f3¯{\overline{e_{2}}\to\overline{f_{3}}} in some order. After the flip e2¯→f3¯{\overline{e_{2}}\to\overline{f_{3}}}, also the flip g8→f4¯{g_{8}\to\overline{f_{4}}} becomes possible. This gives a total of three different flip sequences that perform the flips e4→f2{e_{4}\to f_{2}}, e2¯→f3¯{\overline{e_{2}}\to\overline{f_{3}}}, and g8→f4¯{g_{8}\to\overline{f_{4}}}, respecting that the last flip has to occur after the middle flip. All result in the same situation with two edges of TFT_{F} being crossed twice by two edges of TIT_{I}.

In the second tree in the fourth row, we have so far added the edges f4f_{4}, f3f_{3} and g8g_{8}. The only edges of TFT_{F} that are not crossed twice are f4¯\overline{f_{4}} and f3¯\overline{f_{3}}. f4¯\overline{f_{4}} can only be added via the flip g8→f4¯{g_{8}\to\overline{f_{4}}} without creating a cycle. f3¯\overline{f_{3}} can be added via the flips e3→f3¯{e_{3}\to\overline{f_{3}}} and e3¯\overline{e_{3}} to f3¯\overline{f_{3}}.

By flipping g8→f4¯{g_{8}\to\overline{f_{4}}}, we can either continue with flipping e3¯→f3¯{\overline{e_{3}}\to\overline{f_{3}}} then e4¯→f2¯{\overline{e_{4}}\to\overline{f_{2}}} or with e3→f3¯{e_{3}\to\overline{f_{3}}} and e4→f3{e_{4}\to f_{3}}. In both cases, we end up with two edges from TIT_{I} being intersected by two edges of TFT_{F}. We cannot add any further edge of TFT_{F} without performing another parking flip.

By flipping e3→f3¯{e_{3}\to\overline{f_{3}}} we are left with two more possible flips, namely g8→f4¯{g_{8}\to\overline{f_{4}}} and e4→f3{e_{4}\to f_{3}}. Any order of the two flips yields a valid flip sequence. Both times we are then left with a situation in which both f4¯\overline{f_{4}} and f1f_{1} from TFT_{F} are crossed by e3¯\overline{e_{3}} and e4¯\overline{e_{4}} from TIT_{I}. We cannot add any further edge of TFT_{F} without performing any further parking flips. A symmetric situation occurs after flipping e3¯→f3¯{\overline{e_{3}}\to\overline{f_{3}}} with the two flips g8→f4¯{g_{8}\to\overline{f_{4}}} and e4¯→f2¯{\overline{e_{4}}\to\overline{f_{2}}}.

We next consider the third tree in the fourth row. We remark that the edge f3¯\overline{f_{3}} splits the tree into two parts. Flips in the two parts can be shuffled arbitrarily. This yields multiple flip sequences that have the same outcome and only differ by the ordering of the flips, more particularly, when the flip g8→f4¯{g_{8}\to\overline{f_{4}}} occurs. In the side of f3¯\overline{f_{3}} that does not contain g8g_{8} there are two flip sequences. Those are e3→f3{e_{3}\to f_{3}} followed by e4→f2{e_{4}\to f_{2}} and e3¯→f3{\overline{e_{3}}\to f_{3}} followed by e4¯→f2¯{\overline{e_{4}}\to\overline{f_{2}}}. Both end in the situation that two edges of TFT_{F} are crossed twice by two edges of TIT_{I}.

In the last tree in the fourth row, we have added the edges f3f_{3} and f4f_{4} of TFT_{F}. The only edges of TFT_{F} that are not crossed twice are f3¯\overline{f_{3}} and f4¯\overline{f_{4}} which are both crossed once by e2¯\overline{e_{2}}. The only possible non-parking flip is e2¯→f4¯{\overline{e_{2}}\to\overline{f_{4}}}. Now the only edge that can be is not crossed twice is f3¯\overline{f_{3}} which can be added by the two flips e3→f3¯{e_{3}\to\overline{f_{3}}} and e3¯→f3¯{\overline{e_{3}}\to\overline{f_{3}}}. e3→f3¯{e_{3}\to\overline{f_{3}}} can only be followed by e2→f2{e_{2}\to f_{2}}, whereas e3¯→f3¯{\overline{e_{3}}\to\overline{f_{3}}} can only be followed by e2¯→f2¯{\overline{e_{2}}\to\overline{f_{2}}}. In both cases we again end up with two edges of TFT_{F} being crossed by two edges of TIT_{I}. ∎
